Screening teams are responsible for ensuring that referrals to these services are provided in a timely manner. Furthermore, any student who is identified as potentially being a danger to self or others requires immediate assessment to ensure safety. These processes emphasize connecting students to available mental health resources while maintaining a focus on timely follow-up and safety assessment.

Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Search Methods A comprehensive literature search of electronic databases was conducted to identify existing, current literature regarding depression screening among college students. The following electronic databases were utilized: CINAHL, PubMed, ProQuest/Medline, ScienceDirect, Ovid, ProQuest Psychology Journals, and PsycARTICLES. Boolean search techniques were used to assist with the search methods, e.g., (depression AND college student) and (university student* OR college student* AND depressi* OR depressive symptom OR depressive disorder AND PHQ-2). Table A1 contains the literature search strategies (see Appendix A). Inclusion criteria were: (1) participants consisted of college or university students of any age; (2) studies included depression and depressive symptoms; (3) studies containing the depression screening tool called the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ); (4) studies published as peer-reviewed; (5) the setting of the studies consisted of a college, university, or primary healthcare setting; (6) studies that included depression screening via the electronic medical record (EMR). Exclusion criteria were: (1) non-college students as participants; (2) languages other than English were restricted; (3) studies before the year 2014 were restricted; (4) studies without reports of depression or depressive symptoms (5) studies whose full texts could not be found.
